prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map depicts an indoor bedroom layout as the camera wearer turns right from a window blinds and nightstand area (frame 1, ~0.3–0.6 m away) toward a room with a left-hand wall, a floor cushion/beanbag (~1.0–1.5 m away below and to the left), a bed (~1.2–2.5 m away to the right), and an open doorway and closet in the background (~3.5–5.0 m away). Across frames 2 to 5, a dog lying on the near left corner of the bed (~1.2–1.8 m from the wearer and ~0.5 m to the right of the floor cushion) appears as a slightly brighter raised contour above the mattress surface, facing toward the camera wearer in frames 2–3 before the wearer steps forward, dips the camera toward the cushion in frame 4 (~0.6–1.0 m, within arm's reach), and turns right toward the bed in frame 5. Only the candle jar and blinds in frame 1 and the left wall and floor cushion in frame 4 are within the camera wearer's arm's reach (~0.3–0.8 m), while no other people are present in the scene. Compared to RGB alone, the depth map clearly separates the foreground furniture, the receding left wall plane, and the deep background doorway/closet cavity, even in dark or low-contrast areas. However, it is unreliable where the dog's silhouette merges smoothly into the bed surface in frames 2, 3, and 5, and where bright window light in frame 1 and dark doorway shadows in frames 2–5 distort true metric depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates discrete foreground regions across the bedroom scene, though no other people are actually present and several masks are misclassified or missing. In frame 1, the cylindrical candle jar on the dark surface (~0.4 m away in front of the wearer, within arm's reach) is falsely labeled as a 'toilet', while the window blinds and phone below it are unsegmented. In frames 2 and 3, the dog lying on the near left corner of the bed (~1.2–1.8 m away, facing and looking toward the camera wearer) is segmented as 'dog' and sits directly atop the bed mask in frame 2 (~0.5 m right of the unsegmented green floor cushion), but in frame 3 the bed mask is erroneously shifted onto the left wall (~0.5–2.0 m away) leaving the actual bed unsegmented around the dog. As the camera wearer moves closer and tilts down in frame 4 before turning right in frame 5, the green floor cushion and white rug (~0.8–1.5 m away) are falsely segmented as a large 'person' mask in frame 4, while frame 5 segments the bed (~1.0–2.5 m away on the right) and two small background regions near the closet/headboard without segmenting the dog lying on the lower edge of the bed. While the map helps delineate the dog's boundary against the patterned bedspread in frames 2 and 3 where RGB textures are busy, it is highly unreliable due to severe class hallucinations ('toilet' for a candle, 'person' for a cushion/rug, 'bed' for a wall) and missing masks for the dog in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is almost entirely blank across the five frames, confirming that no visible people are standing or sitting in the bedroom in front of the camera wearer and no hands enter the egocentric field of view within arm's reach. The only skeleton detection appears in frame 2 at the lower-center right (~1.2–1.6 m from the camera wearer), where a small yellow human body skeleton is falsely fitted onto the dog lying on the near corner of the bed. In that frame, the spurious skeleton places head and shoulder keypoints near the dog's upward-facing head (which looks toward the camera wearer) and torso/hip keypoints along the dog's body (~0.3 m above the floor cushion to its left), while partly occluded lower-limb keypoints trail off near the bottom edge of the frame. As the camera wearer turns and steps forward across frames 3 to 5—passing within arm's reach (~0.5–0.8 m) of the left wall and floor cushion in frame 4 and angling toward the bed in frame 5—no skeletons are detected on the dog or anywhere else in the room. This map adds no true spatial information beyond what is visible in the RGB strip and is unreliable in frame 2 where it mistakes the canine's posture on the bed for a human body skeleton.
